definition: **Architecture Decision Record.** A short document capturing one significant technical decision, its context, and its consequences.
**Application Performance Monitoring.** Server-side instrumentation showing where time is spent inside services. Answers "where is it slow?"
A retrospective norm treating human error as a symptom of system design rather than a cause to be punished.
A pattern that stops calls to a failing dependency so its failure doesn't cascade.
**Dynamic Application Security Testing.** Probing a running application for vulnerabilities.
The reliability an SLO permits you to spend. Exhausting it is the signal to stop shipping features and work on stability.
A runtime switch that enables or disables functionality without a deploy — the fastest mitigation lever available.
The single person coordinating an incident response. Not necessarily the most technical person present; their job is decisions and communication, not debugging.
Mean time to **detect**, **acknowledge**, and **resolve**. See the metrics section for the caveats.
The vendor-neutral standard for emitting metrics, logs and traces, letting you change observability vendors without re-instrumenting.
The 95th or 99th percentile of a distribution. p95 latency of 400ms means 95% of requests finished faster than that. Averages hide the users having the worst time; percentiles don't.
Governs a **class of incident** — roles, phases, communication. Distinct from a runbook.
**Root Cause Analysis.** The formal, structured analysis of why an event occurred. See the caution in Layer 4 about the singular framing.
**Rate, Errors, Duration.** The standard three for a request-driven service.
**Real User Monitoring.** Telemetry from actual browsers and devices. Answers "what did the user see?"
Governs a **known task** — precise commands, expected outputs, abort paths.
**Static Application Security Testing.** Scanning source code for vulnerabilities without running it.
A reconstruction of a user's actual session. Answers "what did the user do?"
The severity scale. See the severity reference table.
The **indicator** you measure, the **objective** you hold yourself to, and the **agreement** with a customer that carries penalties. Internal targets should be stricter than contractual ones.
**Standard Operating Procedure.** Governs a recurring workflow rather than a single task or incident.
Scripted journeys run on a schedule from fixed locations, catching breakage before a real user does.
Manual, repetitive operational work that scales with system size and produces no lasting value. The standing target for automation.
**Utilization, Saturation, Errors.** The standard three for a resource such as CPU, memory or a connection pool.
